items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Ella Fitzgerald always closed the show... Playing for her, we took turns. I’d play the first half. Then Buddy would play the first half the second part of the tour.

ctx.x: You got to see him? Did you see him perform?

I saw him once. He was amazing, not only as a drummer, but – Gene Krupa used to say that in those days, the Savoy Ballroom was open. They used to have a battle of the bands up there. They always put Benny Goodman’s band with Chick Webb’s band, because Chick had Ella Fitzgerald as singer. I saw Gene one time when he was getting ready to do that. He said, “I’m going up to play opposite Chick Webb and get a drum lesson.” He didn’t know a note if it was as big as this room. Yet you could play an arrangement for him,…

items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: Ella Fitzgerald would come on the show, Joe Williams, Tony Bennett, Duke, whoever it was, Dizzy. In and out.

ctx.x: Have you ever had occasion to play with Joe Williams?

Joe Williams? Absolutely. There is an example, well he’s such a great talent, but what makes Joe Williams so great, is not only is he one of the greatest singers in the world, but when he comes in to rehearse, he comes in like a gentleman, he knows exactly what he wants to rehearse, what he wants to work out, he does it, he’s in and out with no problems. That to me is a real artist you know? Because he knows exactly what the band should sound like, what the dynamic should be, what he wants from the drummer, and…

never had trouble with the biggies. Ella Fitzgerald would come on the show, Joe Williams, Tony Bennett, Duke, whoever it was, Dizzy. In and out. It was always that person that didn’t quite make it that — “something is wrong with the dressing room.”
